## Author's thesis (paraphrased from source)

The handbook presents human performance improvement (HPI) as a set of concepts and principles tied to a performance model, not as a programme: "HPI, as described in this handbook and practiced in the field, is not so much a program as it is a distinct way of thinking" [V] (Ch 1, p. 1-1); the Preface sets it apart from programmes "such as Six Sigma, Total Quality Management, and the like" [V] (Preface, p. v). Its central reframing is that human error is a symptom of the system rather than its cause: the system approach treats human error as "not a cause of failure, alone, but rather the effect or symptom of deeper trouble in the system" [V], and "Human error is not random; it is systematically connected to features of people’s tools, the tasks they perform, and the operating environment in which they work" [V] (Preface, p. v). Error comes "not only by normal human fallibility, but also by incompatible management and leadership practices and organizational weaknesses in work processes and values" [V] (Ch 1, p. 1-1).

The strategy has two halves. Individuals and teams anticipate, prevent, catch and recover from active errors at the job site; the organisation identifies and eliminates the latent organisational weaknesses that provoke error and degrade controls [AP] (Ch 1, p. 1-16). The handbook argues that both are needed because they work on different things: "Reducing the error rate minimizes the frequency, but not the severity of events. Only controls can be effective at reducing the severity of the outcome of error" [V] (Ch 1, p. 1-16). It compresses this into a formula, reducing errors (Re) and managing controls (Mc) to reach zero significant events, "Re + Mc → ØE" [V] (Ch 1, p. 1-16). Chapter 3 sharpens the second half: "Error reduction can only reduce the time between events" [V], so verifying the integrity of controls must be one of management's top priorities [AP] (Ch 3, p. 3-3).

Five principles anchor the behaviours the handbook promotes [AP] (Ch 1, p. 1-19): that people are fallible and the best still err; that error-likely situations can be predicted, managed and prevented; that organisational processes and values shape individual behaviour; that reinforcement from leaders, peers and subordinates produces high performance; and that events can be avoided by understanding why mistakes occur and applying the lessons of past events (quoted in full in Part I). The handbook draws two operating consequences that recur through its chapters. First, the response to an error has to match how the error happened: errors made in the skill-based mode are not cured by retraining, rule-based errors may be, and knowledge-based mistakes need analysis (Ch 2, pp. 2-27 to 2-28). Second, the response to an event has to look past the person: "Instead of asking how the individual failed the organization, the question 'how did the organization fail the individual?' would be more appropriate" [V] (Ch 4, p. 4-26).

The handbook places itself inside DOE's Integrated Safety Management (ISM) system and says its tools "cannot compete with ISM, but must support ISM" [V] (Ch 1, p. 1-3). It credits the commercial nuclear industry, and the Institute of Nuclear Power Operations (INPO) in particular, as the source of its content and approach [BT] (Preface, p. v), and in Chapter 5 calls James Reason's work "the foundation for the human performance improvement model" [V] (Ch 5, p. 5-11) that DOE adopted.

## Part I: Framing, ISM integration and the event model (Preface, Ch 1)

### What the handbook is and who it is for

The Preface describes the handbook as a reference for anyone in the DOE community who wants to learn about human performance and how to improve it, addressing the roles of individuals, leaders and the organisation [AP] (Preface, p. v). It defines an event as "an undesirable change in the state of structures, systems, or components or human/organizational conditions (health, behavior, controls) that exceeds established significance criteria" [V] (Preface, p. v). It describes human performance as a system: "The model contends that human performance is a system that comprises a network of elements that work together to produce repeatable outcomes. The system encompasses organizational factors, job-site conditions, individual behavior, and results" [V] (Preface, p. v). A companion Volume 2 covers the methods for catching and reducing errors and locating latent weaknesses [AP] (Preface, p. v).

The Preface says the content draws on practices from the commercial nuclear power industry, that INPO helped DOE roll out its human performance courses "patterned on the INPO model", and that the handbook "reflects heavily" on INPO's *Human Performance Fundamentals Course Reference* (2002) and *Human Performance Reference Manual*, INPO 06-003 (2006) [BT] (Preface, p. v). It introduces high reliability organisations (HROs) as organisations that operate under trying conditions yet have very few accidents, names examples (aircraft carriers, air traffic control, power grid dispatch centres, nuclear submarines, airline cockpit crews, nuclear power plants, offshore platforms), and presents HPI as one approach toward HRO attributes [AP] (Preface, pp. v–vi). It also states what the handbook is not: "This handbook is not a human factors manual" [V], nor a modification of other safety regulations [AP] (Preface, p. vi).

A reading guide recommends chapters by user group (individual contributors; managers, supervisors and HPI leaders; HPI trainers and practitioners), with selected sections of Chapter 2 flagged as "essential reading" [AP] (Preface, p. vi).

### The aim and the attitudes the handbook wants

Chapter 1 defines human performance at its simplest as "a series of behaviors carried out to accomplish specific task objectives (results)" [V] (Ch 1, p. 1-1). It argues that it is hard to anticipate how trivial conditions influence performance, that error-provoking aspects of design, procedures, processes and human nature exist everywhere, and that defence-in-depth with respect to the human element is therefore needed [AP] (Ch 1, p. 1-1). Other high-risk industries (aviation, medicine, commercial nuclear power, the U.S. Navy) have adopted human performance principles, and adopters report improved quality, efficiency and productivity as well as safety [BT] (Ch 1, p. 1-1, endnote 2).

The attitudes and practices the handbook says are needed to control error-provoking situations are: the will to communicate problems and opportunities to improve; "an uneasiness toward the ability to err" [V]; "an intolerance for error traps that place people and the facility at risk" [V]; vigilant situational awareness; rigorous use of error-prevention techniques; and understanding the value of relationships [AP] (Ch 1, p. 1-2).

### Integration with Integrated Safety Management

DOE began ISM in 1996; experience showed its framework remained valid but implementation varied across the complex, and the revitalised ISM Manual draws on two external sources of lessons: HRO research and HPI initiatives in commercial nuclear, the U.S. Navy and others [AP] (Ch 1, p. 1-2). The handbook lists the seven ISM guiding principles (line management responsibility for safety; clear roles and responsibilities; competence commensurate with responsibilities; balanced priorities; identification of safety standards and requirements; hazard controls tailored to the work; operations authorisation) and the five core functions (define the scope of work; analyse the hazards; develop and implement hazard controls; perform work within controls; provide feedback and continuous improvement) [AP] (Ch 1, pp. 1-3 to 1-4). It shows how human error can damage each stage of the ISM cycle; for example, "If the response to the event only focuses on the minor work error, the other contributing errors will not be addressed" [V] (Ch 1, p. 1-5).

A table maps HPI's two objectives, reducing human error and managing controls, against each ISM core function, naming the HPI tools that support each: task preview for defining scope; job-site review, pre-job briefing and questioning attitude for hazard analysis; self-checking, peer check, and procedure use and adherence for implementing controls; the error-reduction tools for performing work; post-job review and the investigation of events triggered by human error for feedback and improvement [AP] (Ch 1, pp. 1-6 to 1-9). The table names the topics a post-job review covers (surprises, usability of work documents, knowledge and skill shortcomings, minor errors, unanticipated job-site conditions, adequacy of tools, quality of planning, adequacy of supervision) and describes event investigation as focusing "on problems beyond the individual" [V] to find latent organisational conditions (Ch 1, p. 1-9). Five HPI leadership behaviours support ISM Guiding Principle 1: facilitate open communication, promote teamwork, reinforce desired behaviours, eliminate latent organisational weaknesses, value prevention of errors [AP] (Ch 1, p. 1-10).

### Perspective on human performance and events

A graphic sets out what the handbook calls known about the role of human performance in events: about 80 percent of events are attributed to human error (closer to 90 percent in some industries) and about 20 percent to equipment failures; of the human-error share, about 70 percent stem from latent organisational weaknesses and about 30 percent from individual workers [BT] (Ch 1, p. 1-10, endnote 5 to Perrow and Reason). It reports INPO's finding that three of every four significant events in commercial nuclear power between 1995 and 1999 were attributed to human error, and a Nuclear Regulatory Commission review finding human error a common factor in 21 of 26 fuel-damaging events [BT] (Ch 1, p. 1-10). It lists the costs of a major accident and adds that errors in non-safety tasks (security, work control, cost and schedule, procurement, quality assurance) also cost operations [AP] (Ch 1, pp. 1-10 to 1-11).

The handbook frames against a "traditional belief" that human performance is worker-focused, a belief that "promotes the notion that failures are introduced to the system only through the inherent unreliability of people" [V] (Ch 1, p. 1-11), whereas experience indicates that weaknesses in organisational processes and cultural values are involved in most facility events, so the organisational context of human performance is an important consideration [AP] (Ch 1, p. 1-11).

### Engineers, knowledge workers and the "paper plant"

An NRC study by INEEL found human error a causal factor in 79 percent of licensee events, with four latent failures for every active failure, and design and design-change problems a factor in 81 percent of human-error events; INPO responded with tools for engineers and knowledge workers, many incorporated into DOE's tools manual [BT] (Ch 1, p. 1-11, endnotes 8 and 9). Citing research at one DOE site, the handbook says engineers tend to be critical of others but not self-critical, so their errors may go undetected for years and the chance of learning is reduced; techniques for this group should focus on errors in the knowledge-based mode [BT] (Ch 1, p. 1-11, endnote 10).

The work place or job site is any location where the physical plant or the "paper" plant can be changed, the paper plant being "the aggregate of all the documentation that helps control the configuration of the physical plant" [V] (Ch 1, p. 1-11). Front-line workers touch the physical plant; engineers and technical staff alter the paper plant; managers influence behaviour by directives and example; "The activities of all these individuals need to be controlled" [V] (Ch 1, p. 1-12).

The handbook defines its three actors [AP] (Ch 1, p. 1-12): the individual (any employee, from new hire to senior vice president); the leader (anyone who takes personal responsibility for their own and the facility's performance and tries to influence the organisation's processes and values; managers may not show leadership, and workers can be influential leaders; "The designation as a leader is earned from subordinates, peers, and superiors" [V]); and the organisation (a group with a shared mission, resources and plans that directs people's behaviour, usually through processes and value systems).

### Performance is behaviour plus results

Because good results can come from questionable behaviour and bad results from compliant behaviour (following an incorrectly written procedure), the handbook defines human performance as "behavior plus results (P = B + R)" [V] (Ch 1, p. 1-12; formula credited to Gilbert, endnote 11). Behaviour is observable and measurable, and consistent behaviour is necessary for consistent results; a youth baseball coach cannot shout "throw strikes" but must teach techniques and follow with coaching and reinforcement [AE] (Ch 1, p. 1-13). Results are the outcomes of behaviour; event-free performance depends on reducing error where people touch the facility and where they touch the paper, and on the integrity of controls against residual errors [AP] (Ch 1, p. 1-13).

### Anatomy of an Event

Events are typically triggered by human action, most often in error, but the action could have been directed by a procedure or be a violation [AP] (Ch 1, p. 1-14). The "Anatomy of an Event" graphic links vision, beliefs and values, and mission, goals, policies, processes and programmes, to latent organisational weaknesses, which create error precursors and flawed controls, which with an initiating action produce the event; "Breaking the linkages may prevent events" [V] (Ch 1, p. 1-14). The elements are defined:

- **Event:** an unwanted, undesirable change in the state of structures, systems or components or human or organisational conditions that exceeds significance criteria; other definitions include an outcome that must be undone and "a difference between what is and what ought to be" [V] (Ch 1, p. 1-14).
- **Initiating action:** an action by an individual, correct, in error or in violation, that results in an event. "An error is an action that unintentionally departs from an expected behavior. A violation is a deliberate, intentional act to evade a known policy or procedure requirement and that deviates from sanctioned organizational practices" [V] (Ch 1, p. 1-14). Active errors have immediate, observable, undesirable outcomes; most initiating actions are active errors, so the strategy should include anticipating and preventing them [AP] (Ch 1, p. 1-14).
- **Flawed controls:** defects that, under the right circumstances, may inhibit defences from protecting equipment or people or fail to prevent active errors; "When an event occurs, there is either a flaw with existing controls or appropriate controls are not in place" [V] (Ch 1, p. 1-15).
- **Error precursors:** "unfavorable prior conditions at the job site that increase the probability for error during a specific action; that is, error-likely situations" [V]; an error-likely situation typically exists "when the demands of the task exceed the capabilities of the individual or when work conditions aggravate the limitations of human nature" [V]; they are also known as error traps (Ch 1, p. 1-15).
- **Latent organisational weaknesses:** hidden deficiencies in management control processes (strategy, policies, work control, training, resource allocation) or values (shared beliefs, attitudes, norms, assumptions) that create conditions that provoke errors and degrade controls [BT] (Ch 1, p. 1-15, endnote 15 to Reason). Managers and supervisors should therefore work with the same uneasy respect for error-prone environments as workers, and identifying and eliminating these weaknesses is a second strategic thrust [AP] (Ch 1, p. 1-15).

### The strategic approach

The two challenges are to "Anticipate, prevent, catch, and recover from active errors at the job site" [V] and to "Identify and eliminate latent organizational weaknesses that provoke human error and degrade controls against error and the consequences of error" [V] (Ch 1, p. 1-16). Even when opportunities to err are systematically identified, "people may still err in unanticipated and creative ways" [V], so defence-in-depth (layered controls, so that if one fails others still function) is needed [AP] (Ch 1, p. 1-16).

**Reducing error** focuses on work execution, where workers touch equipment and knowledge workers touch the paper; the objective is to anticipate, prevent or catch active errors "especially at critical steps, where error-free performance is absolutely necessary" [V] (Ch 1, p. 1-16). Opportunities lie in three phases [AP] (Ch 1, pp. 1-16 to 1-17): preparation (planning, job-site reviews and walkdowns, task assignment, task previews and pre-job briefings); performance (working "with a sense of uneasiness" [V], situational awareness, rigorous use of tools, avoiding at-risk practices, quality supervision and teamwork); and feedback (reporting on work preparation and conditions, and behaviour observations with coaching).

**Managing controls.** Events involve breaches in controls; "The top priority to ensure safety from human error is to identify, assess, and eliminate hazards in the workplace" [V], and the most important part of the strategy is "an assertive and ongoing verification and validation of the health of controls" [V] (Ch 1, p. 1-17). Four general types of control are previewed [AP] (Ch 1, pp. 1-17 to 1-18): control of hazards by elimination or substitution; engineered features; administrative provisions; cultural norms; and oversight, in which accountability rests on a "social contract" between workers and management "where a “just culture” prevails" [V]: "In a just culture, people who make honest errors and mistakes are not blamed while those who willfully violate standards and expectations are censured" [V] (Ch 1, p. 1-18). A footnote gives the worker-safety hierarchy of controls: elimination or substitution, engineering controls, work practices and administrative controls, then personal protective equipment, referring to 10 CFR Part 851 [BT] (Ch 1, p. 1-17, footnote *5).

### The five principles of human performance

The handbook calls these the principles or underlying truths of human performance, the foundation for every behaviour it promotes (Ch 1, p. 1-19):

1. "People are fallible, and even the best people make mistakes." [V] (Ch 1, p. 1-19). Error is universal; "No amount of counseling, training, or motivation can alter a person's fallibility" [V] (Ch 1, p. 1-19). The handbook supports the point with a quotation from James Reason's *Human Error* on awareness of the factors that shape error as the first step in error management [BT] (Ch 1, p. 1-19).
2. "Error-likely situations are predictable, manageable, and preventable." [V] (Ch 1, p. 1-19). Specific errors are preventable even though error in general is not; the example is writing the previous year on a cheque early in a new year; by changing the work situation to remove conditions that provoke error, task and individual factors can be managed [AP] (Ch 1, p. 1-19).
3. "Individual behavior is influenced by organizational processes and values." [V] (Ch 1, p. 1-19). Management has historically focused on the "individual error-prone or apathetic workers" [BT] (endnote 17 to Reason), but work is achieved within organisational processes, culture and management systems, and "It is exactly these phenomena that contribute most of the causes of human performance problems and resulting facility events" [V] (Ch 1, p. 1-19).
4. "People achieve high levels of performance because of the encouragement and reinforcement received from leaders, peers, and subordinates." [V] (Ch 1, p. 1-20). "The organization is perfectly tuned to get the performance it receives from the workforce" [V]; positive and immediate reinforcement for expected behaviours is ideal [AP] (Ch 1, p. 1-20).
5. "Events can be avoided through an understanding of the reasons mistakes occur and application of the lessons learned from past events (or errors)." [V] (Ch 1, p. 1-20). Improvement has traditionally been reactive, through corrective actions from event analysis; the handbook calls for combining proactive and reactive approaches, and calls anticipation "a more cost-effective means of preventing events" [V] (Ch 1, p. 1-20).

## Part II: Reducing error (Ch 2)

### Human fallibility and the traps of human nature

Chapter 2 opens by saying the first part of the chapter explores the part of human nature that errs, so that people can better compensate for error through error-reduction tools and improved controls [AP] (Ch 2, p. 2-1). Imprecision is innate: "Unlike a machine that is precise—each time, every time—people are imprecise, especially in certain situations" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-1). Susceptibility to error grows when people work within complex systems that have "concealed weaknesses—latent conditions that either provoke error or weaken controls against the consequences of error" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-1).

People overestimate their ability to maintain control, for two reasons: consequential error is rare, so people reason that errors will be caught or won't matter; and there is a general lack of appreciation of the limits of human capability, so adverse conditions (insufficient rest, distraction, extreme heat or noise) "become normalized and accepted by the individual" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-1). The common traps the handbook describes [AP] (Ch 2, pp. 2-1 to 2-4) are: stress (normal and sometimes helpful, but cumulative; memory lapses are among the first symptoms); avoidance of mental strain, which produces mental shortcuts, defined as assumptions, habit, confirmation bias, similarity bias, frequency bias and availability bias [BT] (endnotes 2–5); limited working memory, whose limits "are at the root of forgetfulness; forgetfulness leads to omissions when performing tasks" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-2), offset by place-keeping; limited attention resources, offset by self-checking (Stop, Think, Act, Review); mind-set, where a focus on the goal "tends to conceal hazards, leading to inaccurate perception of risks" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-3), offset by mindful pre-job briefings; difficulty seeing one's own error, offset by peer-checking and verification; limited perspective ("bounded rationality") [BT] (endnote 11 to Simon); susceptibility to emotional and social factors such as pride and embarrassment; fatigue; and presenteeism.

### Unsafe attitudes and risk perception

Attitudes are learned and can be chosen [AP] (Ch 2, p. 2-4). "People in general are poor judges of risk and commonly underestimate it" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-4). People think of risk as likelihood and neglect severity, and they fear risks less when they feel in control, gain a benefit, live with the hazard, choose it, find it routine, trust its source, are unaware of it, see it as natural, or when it affects others [BT] (Ch 2, pp. 2-4 to 2-5, endnote 16). "Awareness of these unsafe, detrimental attitudes among the workforce is a first step toward applying error-prevention methods" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-5).

The handbook names six unsafe attitudes, each with a historical example [AE] (Ch 2, pp. 2-5 to 2-6): **pride** (MacArthur's refusal to admit error at the 1951 hearings); **heroic** (Custer at Little Big Horn; heroic reactions are impulsive, with "an extreme focus on the goal without consideration of the hazards to avoid" [V]); **fatalistic** (trench warfare in the First World War, illustrated with a quoted passage, paraphrased here [BT]); **invulnerability** (the *Titanic*'s lifeboats: "Error is always a surprise when it happens" [V]); **Pollyanna** (presuming all is normal, "What can go wrong?" or "It's routine."); and **bald tire**, "A belief that past performance is justification for not changing (improving) existing practices or conditions" [V]; "Managers can be tempted to ignore recommendations for improvement if results have been good" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-6).

The bald-tire example is the Columbia space shuttle: over 22 years some foam fell from the external tank and struck the shuttle on every flight; "Foam strikes were normalized to the point where they were simply viewed as a “maintenance” issue—a concern that did not threaten a mission’s success" [V]; in 2003, even after launch video showed a strike unlike any before, programme managers were not unduly alarmed, and "Learned attitudes about foam strikes diminished management’s wariness of their danger" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-6, endnote 23 to the Columbia Accident Investigation Board Report, 7.2).

### At-risk behaviours

At-risk behaviours are "actions that involve shortcuts, violations of error-prevention expectations, or simple actions intended to improve efficient performance of a task, usually at some expense of safety" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-6). They are not necessarily dangerous, but workers and managers should know which occur, when and on which systems [AP] (Ch 2, p. 2-6). They are rarely penalised and are reinforced by convenience, comfort and time saved [BT] (Ch 2, pp. 2-6 to 2-7, endnote 24 to Geller). Examples include hurrying, cookbook-style procedure use, removing several tags without annotating, one-person critical steps without peer checking, skipping a procedure on a "routine" task, multitasking and signing off steps before doing them; risky behaviours at DOE sites have contributed to injuries and deaths (hot electrical panels, fall protection, lasers, forklifts, unknown tank contents) [AE] (Ch 2, p. 2-7). "Persistent use of at-risk behaviors builds overconfidence and trust in personal skills and ability" [V]; without correction they become automatic, risk is underestimated, and eventually an event occurs, so "Managers and supervisors must provide specific feedback when at-risk behavior is observed" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-7).

### Error types: slips, lapses, mistakes, violations

The handbook's error taxonomy (Ch 2, pp. 2-8 to 2-11):

- **Error.** "People do not err intentionally. Error is a human action that unintentionally departs from an expected behavior" [V]; "Error is behavior without malice or forethought; it is not a result" [V]; it is "provoked by a mismatch between human limitations and environmental conditions at the job site, including inappropriate management and leadership practices and organizational weaknesses that set up the conditions for performance" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-8).
- **Slips and lapses.** "Slips occur when the physical action fails to achieve the immediate objective. Lapses involve a failure of one’s memory or recall" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-8). The ways an action can go wrong are listed by timing, duration, sequence, object, force, direction, speed and distance [BT] (Ch 2, p. 2-8, endnote 27 to Hollnagel).
- **Mistakes.** "Mistakes, by contrast, occur when a person uses an inadequate plan to achieve the intended outcome. Mistakes usually involve misinterpretations or lack of knowledge" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-8). The glossary defines a mistake as an error made "because the intent of the act was incorrect for the work situation" [V] (Glossary, p. vi).
- **Active errors** are "observable, physical actions that change equipment, system, or facility state, resulting in immediate undesired consequences" [V]; front-line workers commit most of them because they touch equipment, and most are trivial and easily recovered [AP] (Ch 2, p. 2-8).
- **Latent errors** "result in hidden organization-related weaknesses or equipment flaws that lie dormant" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-9). They have no immediate outcome, include decisions that create preconditions for error or fail to catch it, and can be created by managers, supervisors, technical staff and front-line workers (an incorrect gasket, a mispositioned valve, a wrong label); "Usually, there is no immediate feedback that an error has been made" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-9). A comparison table sets active errors (workers; equipment; immediate; visible) against latent errors (managers, engineers, workers, corporate and support staff; paper, values and beliefs; delayed or dormant; not visible) [AP] (Ch 2, p. 2-9). "As one can see from the table, latent errors are more subtle and threatening than active errors" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-9). An NRC study of 35 events found that of 270 errors, 81 percent were latent and 19 percent active, with design and maintenance errors the largest contributors [BT] (Ch 2, pp. 2-9 to 2-10, endnote 31).
- **Violations** are "the intentional (with forethought) circumvention of known rules or policy" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-10). "Most violations are well intentioned, arising from a genuine desire to get a job done according to management’s wishes" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-10, the sentence carries endnote 32 to the UK Health and Safety Executive). Violations are rarely sabotage; "The deliberate decision to violate a rule is a motivational or cultural issue" [V], and willingness to violate depends on the practices and values of the work group and its leadership, the individual's character, or both [AP] (Ch 2, p. 2-10). Violations are usually for convenience, expedience or comfort; goal conflicts and the aftermath of a previous mistake tempt people to violate [AP] (Ch 2, p. 2-10). A research list gives the circumstances that prompt violations in order of influence, from low potential for detection and absence of authority through peer pressure, role models, the standard's perceived unimportance to management, competition, obstacles and conflicting goals, to precedent [BT] (Ch 2, p. 2-10, endnote 33 to Reason). The handbook states that its focus is error, not violation: "This handbook focuses on managing human error" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-11).

### Dependency and team errors

"For controls to be reliable, they must be independent; that is, the failure of one does not lead to the failure of another" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-11). Three situations create unhealthy dependency [BT] (Ch 2, p. 2-11, endnote 34 to the HSE): equipment dependencies (lowered vigilance because hardware is assumed to work; the worker can become a "common mode failure" across redundant trains [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-11)); team errors; and personal dependencies (reliance on one's own experience; "Competence does not guarantee positive control" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-15)). Remedies for equipment dependency include forcing functions and interlocks, staggering work on redundant equipment, diversifying equipment and training on failure modes [AP] (Ch 2, pp. 2-11 to 2-12).

A team error is "a breakdown of one or more members of a work group that allows other individual members of the same group to err—due to either a mistaken perception of another’s abilities or a lack of accountability within the individual’s group" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-12). A logic example shows a supervisor's independent check giving one-in-a-million error likelihood, falling to one in a thousand if the supervisor assumes competence and does not check [BT] (Ch 2, p. 2-12, endnote 35). Named team-error dynamics [AP] (Ch 2, pp. 2-13 to 2-15): halo effect (operating rooms); pilot/co-pilot deference, with Air Florida Flight 90 (1982) as the example, where the co-pilot flagged anomalous engine readings at least five times but did not oppose the captain's decision to take off [AE]; free riding, with Bhopal (1984) as the example, where an operator testified that it "was not my job" to act on an unsealed valve [AE]; groupthink, with eight symptoms adapted from Janis [BT]; and diffusion of responsibility, which "often causes a “risky shift” in decision-making and problem resolution" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-15), with a late-1980s DOE pump replacement in which a group of supervisors bypassed work control, quality and labour rules under schedule pressure, something no one of them would have done alone [AE] (Ch 2, p. 2-15, endnote 43 notes the writer worked at the Hanford site at the time). Strategies to reduce team errors include freedom of thought, challenging others' actions and assumptions, training on team errors, a devil's advocate, timeouts, and an independent task preview before the pre-job briefing [AP] (Ch 2, p. 2-15). Overcoming personal dependencies involves training on the limits of human nature, a culture of situational awareness and questioning, coaching tool use in the field, and knowledge of critical steps [AP] (Ch 2, p. 2-16).

### Information processing, memory and attention

The handbook summarises a three-store memory model (sensory, short-term or working, long-term) with shared attention resources, credited to Wickens [BT] (Ch 2, pp. 2-16 to 2-18), and describes two control modes, the conscious (restricted, slow, sequential, error-prone, "but potentially very smart" [V]) and the automatic (largely unconscious, fast, parallel, effortless, knowing "only what it knows" [V]) (Ch 2, p. 2-17, endnote 47 to Reason). When people err, the fault typically lies in sensing, thinking, acting or attention [BT] (Ch 2, p. 2-18). Attention can be focused, divided or selective; "Avoiding error is not as simple as telling someone to “pay attention.”" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-19), because attention is limited, takes in a small share of available data, and is captured by unrelated matters; so it matters to control the work environment by minimising interruptions and distractions [AP] (Ch 2, p. 2-19).

### Performance modes: skill-, rule- and knowledge-based

The handbook adopts Rasmussen's Skill, Rule, Knowledge (SRK) classification, under which the level of performance depends on familiarity with the task and the attention applied [BT] (Ch 2, p. 2-19), and Reason's Generic Error Model System (GEMS), which shows how people move between levels as a task proceeds [BT] (Ch 2, p. 2-20; the flowchart survives only as fragments in the conversion). A driving example illustrates all three levels [BT] (Ch 2, p. 2-20).

- **Skill-based performance** involves "highly practiced, largely physical actions in very familiar situations in which there is little conscious monitoring" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-21). "The error mode for skill-based performance is inattention" [V]; "Skill-based errors are primarily execution errors, involving action slips and lapses in attention or concentration" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-22). Examples include an electrician who, after changing a bulb, out of habit pushed a switch he knew it was unsafe to activate [AE] (Ch 2, p. 2-22). Under ideal conditions the error chance is under 1 in 10,000; about 90 percent of daily activity is skill-based, but only 25 percent of errors in nuclear power are skill-based [BT] (Ch 2, p. 2-23, endnotes 66–68). The tools suggested are task preview, job-site review, questioning attitude, stop when unsure, self-checking, pre-job briefing, place-keeping, peer check and concurrent verification, with self-check as the primary tool [AP] (Ch 2, p. 2-23, footnote *6).
- **Rule-based performance** applies memorised or written rules in an IF-THEN logic when the situation has changed; "the prevalent error mode is misinterpretation" [V], and errors involve "deviating from an approved procedure, applying the wrong response to a work situation, or applying the correct procedure to the wrong situation" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-24). Examples include the two small green cars and a London rail crash (1988) caused by an untrained technician's "strong but wrong rules" [BT] (Ch 2, p. 2-24, endnote 74). The error chance rises to roughly 1 in 1,000, and about 60 percent of errors in nuclear power are rule-based [BT] (Ch 2, p. 2-24, endnotes 75–76). Tools include task preview, procedure adherence, pre-job briefing, questioning attitude, peer-checking and concurrent verification, with procedure use and adherence as primary [AP] (Ch 2, pp. 2-24 to 2-25, footnote *7).
- **Knowledge-based performance** is a response to a totally unfamiliar situation with no recognisable skill or rule [AP] (Ch 2, p. 2-25). The handbook warns against equating it with work done by highly educated people: "The situation described as “knowledge based mode” might better be called “lack of knowledge” mode" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-25). Problem solvers tend to use only readily available information, "often become over-confident in the correctness of their knowledge; an “I know I’m right” effect" [V], and become enmeshed in one aspect of the problem [BT] (Ch 2, p. 2-26, endnote 82 to Embrey); "Consequently, the prevalent error mode is an inaccurate mental model of the system, process, or facility status" [V]; the error chance is roughly one in two to one in ten, and about 15 percent of errors in nuclear power are knowledge-based [BT] (Ch 2, pp. 2-26 to 2-27, endnotes 83–84). Examples of knowledge-based activities include troubleshooting, engineering evaluation of a new design, meetings to address problems, scientific experiments, root cause analysis, planning business strategies, making budget allocation decisions, allocating resources and changing policies and expectations [AP] (Ch 2, p. 2-26). Tools include technical task pre-job briefing, project planning, problem-solving, decision-making and peer review [AP] (Ch 2, p. 2-27).

### Matching the corrective action to the performance mode

This section is the handbook's statement of how the response to an error should depend on the kind of error. Knowing the performance mode the person was in "is instructive" when an error of consequence needs corrective action [AP] (Ch 2, p. 2-27). Workers doing rule-based work need accurate, complete procedures and access to experts; skill-based workers need adequate tools, freedom from interruptions and distractions, and simple job aids; knowledge-based work needs "collaboration with a small team of thoughtful, committed, and experienced individuals" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-27).

- **Skill-based slips and lapses: not retraining.** "All too often, workers involved in skill-based performance who err are scheduled for retraining as a logical solution. But, retraining workers to do work that is already basically memorized and automatic, performed with little conscious thought because of the nature of the work, is a waste of time and is an insult to the worker. It is very hard to train a worker not to repeat something he or she did not intend to do in the first place. Training is not the solution in these instances" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-27). Instead, observations gather data about worker behaviours, job-site conditions and missing organisational support (inadequate tools, incomplete packages, poor procedures, noise, heat, lighting), and one-on-one time learns the circumstances of the slip; fatigue, stress, complacency, distractions and interruptions may have provoked it, and "Those conditions can be controlled" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-27).
- **Rule-based errors: retraining may help.** "Errors that occur when working in rule-based performance may be corrected through retraining" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-27), because the worker has misinterpreted a rule or applied a bad rule or a good rule in the wrong place, and understanding requirements is cognitive and must be learned [AP] (Ch 2, p. 2-28). They can also be caught by a questioning attitude, a time out, stopping when unsure, or a peer check [AP] (Ch 2, p. 2-28).
- **Knowledge-based mistakes: analysis first.** "Corrective action to reduce knowledge-based mistakes is more complicated. An analysis of what went wrong will need to be carried out to formulate a corrective action" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-28). The cause may be inadequate knowledge (training could help), or adequate knowledge undermined by weak problem-solving skills, team errors or poor communication; coaching is proactive in any mode and "particularly adept" for knowledge-based work, and peer evaluations are also effective [AP] (Ch 2, p. 2-28).

### Mental models, assumptions, biases and conservative decisions

A mental model is "the structured understanding of knowledge (facts or assumptions) a person has in his or her mind about how something works or operates" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-28). Mental models are used in all modes and help detect slips and lapses; a model may reflect the true, perceived or expected state of a system, and "all mental models are inaccurate to some extent" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-28). In team problem-solving, members should agree the model they will use, and frequent time-outs keep models current [AP] (Ch 2, p. 2-28).

Assumptions reduce mental strain and are sometimes needed to constrain a problem, but they "are treated as fact" too often; phrases such as "I think ...," "We've always …," and "I believe ..." are "danger words" [AP] (Ch 2, p. 2-29). A devil's advocate can challenge assumptions by identifying the conclusion, asking for the data and the reasoning that connects them, inferring beliefs, and testing them with the other person, a process credited to Senge's *Fifth Discipline Fieldbook* [BT] (Ch 2, p. 2-29, endnote 90). Mental biases (confirmation, similarity, frequency, availability, representative and framing) create order amid uncertainty and should be guarded against during troubleshooting and diagnosis [AP] (Ch 2, p. 2-29).

To be conservative "means to be cautious and protective of what is truly important—safety, reliability, quality, security, and so on" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-30). Factors repeatedly mentioned in INPO documents on conservative decisions include recognising challenging conditions, placing systems in a known safe condition when uncertain, seeking expertise, avoiding hasty decisions, rigorously evaluating alternatives, a deliberate decision with abort criteria, and not proceeding in the face of uncertainty [BT] (Ch 2, p. 2-30).

### Error-likely situations and error precursors

An error-likely situation is "A work situation in which there is greater chance for error when performing a specific action or task in the presence of error precursors" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-30). "The simple presence of adverse conditions cannot be error-likely unless a specific action is to occur within that set of adverse conditions" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-30). Error precursors are "unfavorable conditions embedded in the job site that create mismatches between a task and the individual" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-31), organised in four categories [BT] (Ch 2, p. 2-31, endnote 94 to Gilbert): task demands, individual capabilities, work environment and human nature. Because precursors exist before an error, discovering and removing them reduces the chance of error, and people with "an intolerance for error precursors or error traps" [V] report and fix them (an improperly marked valve, a broken ladder, an oil spill) [AE] (Ch 2, p. 2-31).

"Error precursors are not mysterious or obscure. To the contrary, they are noticeable, even obvious, if people look for them" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-32). The handbook gives the eight most common precursors in each category, in order of impact, compiled from a study of INPO's event database [BT] (Ch 2, p. 2-32): task demands (time pressure, high workload, simultaneous multiple actions, repetitive actions or monotony, irreversible actions, interpretation requirements, unclear goals, roles or responsibilities, lack of or unclear standards); individual capabilities (unfamiliarity with the task, lack of knowledge, new techniques, imprecise communication habits, lack of proficiency, indistinct problem-solving skills, unsafe attitudes, illness or fatigue); work environment (distractions and interruptions, changes or departures from routine, confusing displays or controls, workarounds and out-of-service instrumentation, hidden system response, unexpected equipment conditions, lack of alternative indication, personality conflict); human nature (stress, habit patterns, assumptions, complacency or overconfidence, mind-set, inaccurate risk perception, mental shortcuts, limited short-term memory). Some organisations give front-line workers a precursor card for pre-job briefings [AP] (Ch 2, p. 2-32). Worked examples pair an error with its precursors (wrong year on cheques; turning an identical adjacent switch; engine oil poured into a hydraulic system) [AE] (Ch 2, p. 2-33). "Consequently, no work should be considered routine" [V]; most events originate during routine activities, and "A sub-principle of human performance is there are no routine tasks" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-33). Attachments A and B expand the lists and describe the most common precursors [BT] (Ch 2, Att. A–B, pp. 2-35 to 2-43).

### Error-prevention tools, system changes and reporting

There are two ways to keep error from harming the facility: keep people from erring, or keep errors from causing harm (controls) [AP] (Ch 2, p. 2-33). "Human performance tools are designed to help people anticipate, prevent, and catch active errors" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-33), while methods for latent errors aim more to catch than prevent because people are usually unaware when they occur [AP] (Ch 2, p. 2-34). The purpose of the tools, described in Volume 2, is positive control: "what is intended to happen is what happens, and that is all that happens" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-34). Because people still err however rigorously they use tools, the handbook keeps its dual approach, written here as "Re + Mc = ØE" [V] (Ch 2, p. 2-34).

The handbook also recognises a second dimension of error reduction, changing engineered systems so equipment and working conditions support human needs, the province of human factors professionals [AP] (Ch 2, p. 2-34). "Reporting errors and error precursors is an essential behavior needed to acquire feedback from the field about flawed engineered or management systems" [V], and managers should encourage workers to report error-provoking conditions whenever they meet them [AP] (Ch 2, p. 2-34).

## Part III: Managing controls (Ch 3)

### Controls and their failure

The chapter explains that it uses "controls" in place of the "defenses" and "barriers" of the wider literature to align with ISM; the meaning is essentially the same [AP] (Ch 3, p. 3-1). "An accident occurs only when one or more controls have failed; either they did not serve their purpose or they were missing" [V] (Ch 3, p. 3-1). Controls are "any human, technical, or organizational features that protect the facility and personnel against hazards" [BT] (Ch 3, p. 3-1, endnote 2). Chernobyl Unit 4 (1986) is offered as "a classic example of multiple failed or missing controls—some resulting from design flaws and some from the errors of operators" [V] (Ch 3, p. 3-1): operators continued a test below permitted power, disabled emergency cooling and shutdown systems, and withdrew control rods beyond limits, and the design lacked containment [AE] (Ch 3, p. 3-2). Everyday controls (fire-resistant materials, smoke alarms, traffic lights, seatbelts, rumble strips) illustrate the idea [AE] (Ch 3, pp. 3-2 to 3-3).

### Severity and the organisation's role

"The significance, or severity, of a particular event lies in the consequences suffered by the physical plant or personnel, not the error that initiated the event" [V] (Ch 3, p. 3-3). The same error can be one of hundreds without consequence or the trigger of a serious accident; "For a significant event to occur, multiple breakdowns in controls or barriers must first occur. Whereas human error typically triggers an event, it is the number of controls and the weaknesses of those controls that dictate the severity of the event" [V] (Ch 3, p. 3-3). Flawed controls are attributable to organisational weaknesses, so "to focus only on error reduction to prevent events is a bad strategy" [V] (Ch 3, p. 3-3). "Significant events triggered by human error are rightfully characterized as organizational failures" [V] (Ch 3, p. 3-3).

### Defence functions and reliability

Controls serve six functions [BT] (Ch 3, p. 3-4, endnote 5): create awareness, detect and warn, protect, recover, contain, and enable escape, each with examples. Controls are more reliable when they do not depend on people: engineered controls such as interlocks are more reliable than administrative ones such as procedures, tools and training, and "If it is imperative to prevent error, then physical, engineered controls are more appropriate" [V] (Ch 3, p. 3-5).

### Defence-in-depth: four lines of control

"Controls themselves are not necessarily perfect. Multiple, overlapping controls are needed to compensate for this reality" [V] (Ch 3, p. 3-5). Four types work together (Ch 3, pp. 3-5 to 3-12):

- **Engineered controls** act actively (pumps, valves) or passively (pipes, vessels, berms); the most reliable are passive because they need no operational support [AP] (Ch 3, p. 3-5). Elements of effective engineered controls include human-centred design, eliminating unnecessary interactions, interlocks and error-tolerant design, and fixing workarounds and labelling; common flaws include out-of-service equipment, workarounds, nuisance alarms, noise, missing labels, poor lighting and awkward layout [AP] (Ch 3, pp. 3-5 to 3-6).
- **Administrative controls** such as procedures "inform people about what to do, when to do it, where it is to be done, and how well to do it" [V] and rely on human judgment, so they are less reliable than engineered controls [AP] (Ch 3, p. 3-6). Common flaws include two actions in one procedure step, vague expectations, superficial document reviews, critical steps not identified, backlogs, packages without operating experience, insufficient staffing and routine overtime leading to fatigue, and too little time for field supervision [AP] (Ch 3, pp. 3-7 to 3-8).
- **Cultural controls.** "An effective safety culture engenders the belief that when production and safety conflict, safety will prevail" [V] (Ch 3, p. 3-8). "What an organization says its values are may not be reflected in its behavior" [V] (Ch 3, p. 3-8); its true values show in the observed acts of its people, especially managers [BT] (endnote 8). Beliefs with positive impact include that absolutely safe environments do not exist, human beings are fallible, people want to do a good job, human error is normal, there is no routine task, significant events are organisational failures, and error is an opportunity to learn [AP] (Ch 3, p. 3-9). Attitudes that promote safe work are uneasiness toward fallibility, a questioning attitude, a conservative approach, and avoiding unsafe attitudes [AP] (Ch 3, p. 3-9). "A person’s peer group is the largest, single determinant of an individual’s behavior on the job" [V] (Ch 3, p. 3-9); norms are enforced by how peers respond when one is broken [BT] (endnote 9). Flawed cultural controls include reluctance to challenge others, careless tool use, inconsistency between what managers say and what they reward, uncritical observation comments, "initiating disciplinary action for honest mistakes" [V], and bonuses based only on productivity [AP] (Ch 3, p. 3-10).
- **Oversight controls.** "The very nature of latent conditions is such that they will not self-reveal, they must be discovered" [V] (Ch 3, p. 3-10). Oversight aims to make the facility resilient to significant events, that is, to minimise severity, by seeing what is actually going on, identifying gaps, acting on them and verifying resolution [AP] (Ch 3, pp. 3-10 to 3-11). A standing Human Performance Steering Committee of the senior team sets vision and strategy and promotes accountability [AP] (Ch 3, p. 3-11). Flawed oversight includes irregular committee meetings, self-assessments that miss important attributes, insufficient trending, a lack of field observations, and "Root cause analyses are shallow and focus on individual errors without addressing organizational contributors to events" [V] (Ch 3, p. 3-11). A Human Performance Improvement Plan is a living plan reviewed at every committee meeting [AP] (Ch 3, p. 3-12).

### The Performance Model

Human performance can be considered a system, and systems thinking "involves pondering the multiple causes and effects, the variables that come to bear on the worker at the point of touching equipment in the facility" [V] (Ch 3, p. 3-12). Restating the third principle, the handbook says performance occurs within the confines of the organisation, and people will never perform better than the organisation supports [BT] (Ch 3, p. 3-12, endnote 10). "Events are not so much the result of error-prone workers as they are the outcome of error-prone tasks and error-prone work environments, which are controlled by the organization" [V] (Ch 3, p. 3-12; the sentence carries endnote 11 to Reason). Organising means determining the division of labour and coordinating effort through work processes (formal) and culture (informal) [AP] (Ch 3, p. 3-13).

The Performance Model is "a simple, cause-and-effect model" [V] in which organisational processes and values, shaped by leadership, create job-site conditions, which shape worker behaviours, which produce plant results (Ch 3, p. 3-14). Organisational factors encompass all the ways management directs and coordinates work, and show up in the four kinds of control; for a specific task they "create a unique array of job-site conditions (work environment)—good or bad—that set people up for either success or failure" [V] (Ch 3, p. 3-14). Job-site conditions combine environmental factors (procedure quality, labelling, interface, heat) and individual factors (knowledge, experience, family problems, colour blindness), and error precursors are the subset that provokes error [AP] (Ch 3, pp. 3-14 to 3-15). The handbook sets a quotation from Reason's *Human Error* beside this section on changing the conditions under which people work rather than the human condition [BT] (Ch 3, p. 3-15). Plant results depend on the presence, integrity and effectiveness of both processes and controls [AP] (Ch 3, p. 3-15).

### Managing controls: the Performance Improvement Model

The handbook calls "a faulty assumption" the belief that people can always distinguish right from wrong and lack motivation when they act carelessly; error-prone tasks and environments are usually created by latent organisational weaknesses [AP] (Ch 3, p. 3-15). "Latent errors or conditions are difficult to prevent. Once they are created they do not fade away, but rather they accumulate in the system" [V], so management's challenge is to limit how long these vulnerabilities exist, and efforts to shorten the duration of latent errors are expected to contribute more to safety than efforts to reduce their frequency [BT] (Ch 3, p. 3-16, endnote 18 to Reason). Because significant events are few, performance information has to come from other, pre-existing sources (field observations, self-assessments, benchmarking, apparent-cause evaluations, trending) [AP] (Ch 3, p. 3-16). Performance improvement has three activities, performance monitoring, analysing and planning solutions, and implementing solutions, shown in a Performance Improvement Model (whose graphic survives only as fragments) [AP] (Ch 3, pp. 3-16 to 3-17).

### Methods for finding latent organisational conditions

The handbook lists self-assessments, performance indicators, trending, benchmarking, operating experience, independent oversight, behaviour observations, problem reporting, problem (causal) analysis, management oversight, surveys and questionnaires, the corrective action program and event investigation [AP] (Ch 3, p. 3-17), and points to Volume 2 section 3 for detail [AP] (Ch 3, p. 3-18).

- **Self-assessments** compare actual with expected performance; the gap is more likely to point to job-site conditions, inadequate processes or weak values than to worker shortfalls [AP] (Ch 3, p. 3-18).
- **Behaviour observations.** "The purpose of an observation is not to criticize or to judge people, but to review the quality and effectiveness of work preparation, policies, and work practices, as well as their implementation" [V] (Ch 3, p. 3-18); the scope should include the whole job and its context, results should be recorded for trending, and "Managers and supervisors must be willing to be critical during an observation" [V] (Ch 3, p. 3-18). "Error rates decrease when managers and supervisors are in the field with workers" [V] (Ch 3, p. 3-19).
- **Problem reporting.** "Workers are in the best position to provide the feedback to help identify latent organizational weaknesses" [V]; post-job reviews provide credible, fresh information and should be quick to do, and "the worker must see appropriate changes in response to his or her feedback" [V] (Ch 3, p. 3-19).
- **Benchmarking**, **performance indicators and trending** (managers "must measure what is important not just what is easy to measure" [V]; indicators listed include event-free days, repeat events, workarounds and backlogs; the Pareto principle helps find the "big hitters") [AP] (Ch 3, pp. 3-19 to 3-20).
- **Operating experience** counters the "It can’t happen here" attitude and is most effective when the right information reaches the right people in time; supervisors should ask workers to explain how they will avoid errors described in past events and elicit work history from experienced workers [AP] (Ch 3, pp. 3-20 to 3-21).
- **Independent oversight** works because an outsider brings "a fresh set of eyes" [V] and can see degraded conditions insiders no longer notice [AP] (Ch 3, p. 3-21).
- **Problem analysis.** "Analysts conducting root cause analysis of significant plant events should focus on what could have prevented the event rather than simply concentrating on who caused an event" [V], and should also determine which controls kept it from being worse (Ch 3, p. 3-22). When causal analysis is fixated on individual culpability, effective corrective actions will be elusive [BT] (Ch 3, p. 3-22, endnote 22). "“Inattention to detail” and “not following procedures” are not root causes even though these are still commonly cited as such in the DOE complex" [V]; a root cause is "the cause that, if corrected, will prevent recurrence of the event" [V] (Ch 3, p. 3-22). Investigations are usually distorted by hindsight, which predisposes the analyst to look for the individual's shortcomings; explaining what people should have done does not explain why they did what they did, so the analyst should work out why the actions made sense at the time, by establishing for each individual their goals, their focus, and what they knew at critical points [BT] (Ch 3, p. 3-22, endnote 23 to Dekker's *Field Guide to Human Error Investigations*). The Anatomy of an Event can also be worked backward from consequences, through initiating actions and precursors and flawed controls, to the organisational weaknesses, so that "the analysis should clearly show the causal links (line of sight) from the organizational weaknesses to the event consequences" [V] (Ch 3, pp. 3-22 to 3-23).
- **Management oversight**, **surveys** (do not ask for input and then fail to act on it), the **Corrective Action Management Program** with its four steps, and **change management**, since "schedule changes are a common contributor to facility events" [V]; change fails most often without a plan covering the problem, current and desired states, new values, responsibility, process, schedule, reinforcement and verification [BT] (Ch 3, pp. 3-23 to 3-24, endnote 27).

Appendix A reports an INPO study of utilities with extended shutdowns, which named nine "warning flags" that let flawed controls accumulate: overconfidence, isolationism, defensive and adversarial relationships, informal operations and weak engineering, production priorities, inadequate change management, unrecognised event significance, ineffective leaders, and lack of self-criticism [BT] (Ch 3, App. A, p. 3-25).

## Part IV: Culture and leadership (Ch 4)

### Organisational and safety culture

The chapter opens with Edgar Schein's account of culture as a pattern of shared basic assumptions learned as a group solves its problems, likened to personality in the individual, and his three levels (artifacts, espoused values, basic underlying assumptions) [BT] (Ch 4, pp. 4-1 to 4-2). The handbook's summary: "Culture is the sum total of the organization’s learning" [V], and in short, "it’s the way we do things around here" [V] (Ch 4, p. 4-2).

A shared belief that the system is robust is dangerous: it leads people to leave defective equipment unfixed, skip procedures, fail to report minor problems, and make non-conservative decisions under uncertainty, so physical, people, learning and "last chance" barriers fail in turn [BT] (Ch 4, p. 4-2, endnote 4 to Packer). Safety is a "collective responsibility in which everyone in the organization shoulders an obligation to ensure that it comes first" [V] (Ch 4, p. 4-3). The handbook cites definitions of safety culture from Jonathan Wert and the British Health and Safety Commission [BT], Reason's "three C's" (commitment, competence, cognizance) [BT], and a Schein remark that creating and managing culture may be the only important thing leaders do [BT] (Ch 4, pp. 4-3 to 4-4). It observes that workers facing incomplete procedures or poor tools regularly trade productivity against protection, especially "when supervisors expect and reward the results and are silent about behaviors needed to stay safe" [V], and that without safety as a demonstrated core value, "managers will unconsciously reinforce getting the job done, with production becoming the default core value" [V] (Ch 4, p. 4-4).

The handbook presents Ron Westrum's view that information flow is the most critical safety-culture issue, with three patterns (pathological, bureaucratic, generative) distinguished by how they treat information and messengers and how they respond to failure; leaders' emphasis determines which use of information predominates [BT] (Ch 4, pp. 4-4 to 4-5). DOE and its contractors adopted a working definition: "An organization’s values and behaviors modeled by its leaders and internalized by its members, which serve to make safe performance of work the overriding priority to protect the workers, public, and the environment" [V] (Ch 4, p. 4-5). Safety-culture attributes adopted from the DOE ISM Manual follow, grouped under leadership (clear expectations and accountability "in the context of a just culture"; management time in the field; conservative decision-making; open communication free from retribution; demonstrated safety leadership; staff development), employee engagement (personal commitment, teamwork, participation in planning, mindfulness of hazards) and organisational learning (performance monitoring, operating experience, trust, questioning attitude, reporting, and effective resolution, where "Even small failures are viewed as windows into the system that can spur learning" [V]) [AP] (Ch 4, pp. 4-6 to 4-10). Under effective resolution, "Error-likely situations are sought out and corrected, and recurrent errors are carefully examined as indicators of latent organizational weaknesses" [V] (Ch 4, p. 4-10). Under conservative decision-making, "Workers are expected and authorized to take conservative actions when faced with unexpected or uncertain conditions" [V], and "The bias is set on proving work activities are safe before proceeding, rather than proving them unsafe before halting. Personnel do not proceed and do not allow others to proceed when safety is uncertain" [V] (Ch 4, p. 4-6).

### Leadership and the production-prevention tension

"A leader is any individual who takes personal responsibility for his or her performance as well as the facility’s performance and attempts to influence the improvement of the organization that supports that performance" [V] (Ch 4, p. 4-11). Focusing on shared assumptions, values and beliefs is perhaps the most effective way to raise resistance to events, but culture is slow to change, while performance, error reduction and process improvement are achievable in the short run [AP] (Ch 4, p. 4-11). Accident research shows "a significant event presents unmistakable evidence of an organizational failure, not simple individual failure" [V]; "Because it takes teamwork to suffer a significant event, it follows that managers, staff, supervisors, and workers have to work together to be free of events" [V] (Ch 4, p. 4-11). The leader's role is to align organisational processes and values to optimise both production and safety [AP] (Ch 4, p. 4-11).

"Production and prevention (error and event) practices always compete in the minds of workers" [V] (Ch 4, p. 4-12). Production outcomes are visible and celebrated; prevention outcomes are "the quiet non-events" [V], so workers can come to see prevention as optional [AP] (Ch 4, p. 4-12). "Production behaviors naturally take precedence over prevention behaviors unless there is a strong safety culture—nurtured by strong leadership" [V]; safety behaviours "do not just happen" [V]; "Therefore, leadership is a defense" [V] and "Leadership is not optional" [V] (Ch 4, p. 4-12).

### Five key leadership practices

Leaders influence performance through five practices [BT] (Ch 4, p. 4-13, endnote 14 to INPO): facilitate open communication; promote teamwork; reinforce desired behaviours; eliminate latent organisational weaknesses; value error prevention.

- **Open communication.** In many major accidents someone knew something that, communicated in time, could have prevented it; the handbook cites this as the basis of the dictum that communication is the most effective defence [BT] (Ch 4, p. 4-13, endnote 15). "If an individual believes his or her errors will be punished, then information related to those errors will likely remain obscure" [V]; "Healthy organizations view error as an opportunity to learn" [V] (Ch 4, p. 4-13).
- **Teamwork.** Teamwork should make individual thinking visible so assumptions can be challenged [AP] (Ch 4, p. 4-13). Aviation research found crew failures in communication, decision-making and leadership in 66 percent of air carrier, 79 percent of commuter and 88 percent of general aviation accidents, which led to Crew Resource Management training; its attributes, carried into the nuclear industry's Control Room Teamwork Development Course, are ask questions, advocate, take initiative, manage conflict, and critique performance [BT] (Ch 4, pp. 4-13 to 4-14, endnote 17).
- **Reinforce expectations.** Behaviour is motivated by its consequences, which reinforce behaviour more than training, directives or threats [BT] (Ch 4, p. 4-14, endnotes 18–19). "All behavior is reinforced. If at-risk behavior is common, it is because management has not made a difference with appropriate negative consequences" [V] (Ch 4, p. 4-15). The handbook presents Daniels's four consequences (positive reinforcement, negative reinforcement, punishment, extinction) and the conditions that make antecedents and reinforcers stronger [BT] (Ch 4, pp. 4-15 to 4-16).
- **Eliminate latent organisational weaknesses**, using the Chapter 3 methods and a systematic performance gap analysis that contrasts current with desired performance and works through a series of diagnostic questions toward corrective actions (adapted from Mager and Pipe; paraphrase only) [BT] (Ch 4, p. 4-16; Att. A, pp. 4-27 to 4-28). The questions cover whether the problem is worth solving, whether direction is clear, whether consequences are appropriate, whether the performer already knows how, and whether other obstacles stand in the way, ending with valid reasons and candidate solutions [BT] (Ch 4, Att. A, pp. 4-27 to 4-28).
- **Value the prevention of error.** Holding high standards regardless of perceived risk makes adherence the norm [AP] (Ch 4, p. 4-17). "The most effective way to communicate values is to act in accordance with them while reinforcing people when they apply them" [V] (Ch 4, p. 4-17); the leader behaviours that convey values, in order of influence, run from what managers pay attention to, measure and control, through reactions to an accident or crisis and resource allocation, to criteria for rewards, punishment, selection and advancement [BT] (Ch 4, p. 4-17, endnote 24 to Schein).

### The Behavior Engineering Model (paraphrase only)

The handbook presents a derivation of Tom Gilbert's Behavior Engineering Model as a structure for identifying the factors that affect performance at the job site and analysing their organisational contributors [BT] (Ch 4, p. 4-17). It sorts job-site conditions into environmental and individual factors and, across each, three headings: direction to act, opportunity to act, and willingness to act [BT] (Ch 4, pp. 4-17 to 4-18). Environmental factors cover job or task information, resources and environment, and incentives and disincentives; individual factors cover knowledge and skills, capacity and readiness, and personal motives; each cell lists conditions for good performance and the relevant error precursors [BT] (Ch 4, pp. 4-19 to 4-22). The handbook argues that environmental factors give the most leverage at the least cost, citing an estimate that 85 percent or more of the causes of facility events originate in organisational processes and culture, and that corrective actions aimed at individual factors have less immediate influence and greater cost [BT] (Ch 4, p. 4-18, endnotes 26–27). It includes the BEM to show that error precursors, like other job-site conditions, are products of organisational processes and values, for example knowledge as an outcome of the training programme [BT] (Ch 4, p. 4-22, endnote 28 to INPO).

### Creating a just culture

**The blame cycle.** The blame cycle is driven by the belief that error happens because people are not properly motivated [BT] (Ch 4, p. 4-23, endnote 29 to Reason). In reality active errors continue however motivated people are, and "Events will continue as long as event investigations stop prematurely at the active human error" [V]; the true causes stay hidden and errors and events persist (Ch 4, p. 4-23). The cycle graphic links human error, individual counselling or discipline, reduced trust, less communication, management less aware of job-site conditions, persisting latent weaknesses, and more flawed defences and precursors [AP] (Ch 4, p. 4-23).

**Categories of violations.** The handbook distinguishes routine violations (corner-cutting at the skill-based level, often prompted by clumsy procedures and seldom sanctioned; they are not necessarily reckless and often look like latent weaknesses) from thrill-seeking or optimising violations, which are reckless [BT] (Ch 4, p. 4-23, endnote 30 to Reason).

**Intent, not consequence.** "In some organizations employees are named, blamed, shamed, and re-trained based on the consequence of their action, not the intent of the action" [V] (Ch 4, p. 4-23), so the same act is punished after an event and ignored without one, and an inadvertent error is treated like a knowing violation [AP] (Ch 4, pp. 4-23 to 4-24). "A just environment is all about getting the balance right between how willful violations and unintentional errors are addressed in the organization" [V]; management sets "a zero tolerance policy for reckless conduct" balanced by confidence that "the vast majority of unintended unsafe acts will go unpunished as honest errors" [V] (Ch 4, p. 4-24).

**Tests.** The Foresight Test asks whether the individual knowingly did something the average peer would recognise as likely to raise the chance of a safety-critical error; impairment, clowning with dangerous equipment, signing off unfinished work and knowingly using substandard parts indicate culpability; the handbook calls it a rule of thumb [BT] (Ch 4, p. 4-24, endnote 31 to Reason and Hobbs). The Substitution Test asks whether a different person with similar skills and training, in the same circumstances as they were perceived at the time, would likely have acted differently; if peers answer "probably not", blame has no place and would obscure systemic deficiencies [BT] (Ch 4, p. 4-25, endnote 32 to Johnston via Reason).

**Culpability Decision Tree.** A logic diagram adapted from Reason helps determine culpability for events or near misses triggered by human error and supports consistent discipline when used with the accountability policy [BT] (Ch 4, p. 4-25). Its questions run through intended actions, intended consequences, knowing violation, whether expectations were available, intelligible, workable and correct, the substitution test, deficiencies in training or selection, history of performance problems, and self-reporting, sorting acts from intentional harm and possible reckless violation through organisationally induced violation and possible negligent error to organisationally induced error, with individual culpability rising on one side and organisational culpability on the other [BT] (Ch 4, p. 4-26). Attachment B explains its use: apply it to each unsafe act separately, use a small team rather than a single manager because the questions are subjective, recognise that unintended actions define slips and lapses (the least blameworthy) and unintended consequences cover mistakes and violations, judge violations by the quality of the procedures, and treat the remaining categories as blameless unless aggravated; experience suggests about 90 percent or more of unsafe acts are blameless [BT] (Ch 4, Att. B, pp. 4-29 to 4-30, endnotes 34–35).

When an honest error triggers an event, the whole supporting system should be evaluated: "Events triggered by human error are often symptomatic of a system failure. Instead of asking how the individual failed the organization, the question 'how did the organization fail the individual?' would be more appropriate" [V]; and "management's first reaction to events should be to look within the organization" [V] (Ch 4, p. 4-26). "A just culture is a prerequisite for a reporting culture" [V] (Ch 4, p. 4-26).

**Reporting culture.** A just environment does not by itself make people report; Attachment C names four barriers (reluctance to confess, fear of the record, scepticism that management will act, effort) and five features of successful reporting programmes (de-identification, protection, separation of functions, feedback, ease of reporting with room to tell a story) [BT] (Ch 4, Att. C, p. 4-31, endnote 36 to Reason). The value of a safety information system lies in identifying recurrent patterns, error traps and weak controls, and its purpose is to learn from near misses, mistakes and inconsequential errors [AP] (Ch 4, Att. C, p. 4-31).

## Part V: Human performance evolution (Ch 5)

### Organisations and where blame has landed

Chapter 5 gives background on the research and concepts that influenced the HPI approach, prompted by lessons from Bhopal, Chernobyl, Challenger, Exxon Valdez and Three Mile Island; "The DOE/INPO HPI approach is one example of how improvement may be achieved" [V] (Ch 5, p. 5-1). People are shaped by the organisations they work in [AP] (Ch 5, p. 5-1). In the Progressive era, corporations reacted to reformers by running safety campaigns that put responsibility for accidents on workers rather than industry [AP] (Ch 5, p. 5-2). "Those who manage organizations, who make the decisions and set the standards for safety, are often removed in time and distance from the consequences of their actions" [V], while workers bear the consequences and may be blamed (Ch 5, p. 5-2). The Morton Thiokol engineers who predicted the Challenger boosters' cold-weather problem are the example, with a quotation from one engineer on responsibility shifting from individuals to institutions [BT] (Ch 5, p. 5-2, endnote 3).

### Influences on HPI

The chapter surveys a series of influences (Ch 5, pp. 5-2 to 5-19):

- **Production** in the Second World War and after, when managers saw themselves as the head and workers as the brawn [AP] (Ch 5, pp. 5-2 to 5-3).
- **Quality management** (Juran, Deming): the shift "from inspection to prevention" [V], quality as everyone's business, worker participation in Quality Circles, customer focus, continuous process improvement driven from the top and implemented from the bottom, and the lesson that "the people closest to the process know best how to improve the process when given a chance to participate" [V] (Ch 5, pp. 5-3 to 5-4).
- **Human factors and ergonomics**: fitting environment and person to each other; Chapanis's 1943 demonstration that "pilot error" fell when cockpit controls were made distinguishable; and Fitts's 1947 study of 460 "pilot errors", many of which were confusions of identical, adjacent flap and gear handles, so that the confusion was systematic, tied to the cockpit layout, rather than random [BT] (Ch 5, p. 5-5, endnote 7 to Dekker).
- **Organisational development** (Lewin, Beckhard, Argyris, Emery) and its interventions such as flatter structures and self-directed teams [BT] (Ch 5, pp. 5-6 to 5-8).
- **Learning organisations**: Senge's five disciplines (systems thinking, personal mastery, mental models, shared vision, team learning), with dialogue and discussion as the two ways teams converse [BT] (Ch 5, pp. 5-8 to 5-10).
- **Human performance technology** as advocated by ISPI: performance analysis, cause analysis and intervention selection [BT] (Ch 5, p. 5-10).
- **Error management**: Reason's theses that error types are tied to normal cognitive processes, that disasters rarely come from one monumental error, that latent conditions combine with local factors and active errors to produce events, that errors are consequences rather than causes of organisational disturbances, and that latent conditions are "resident pathogens" to be removed before an event [BT] (Ch 5, p. 5-11, endnotes 11–13).
- **Mindfulness** (Langer): drawing novel distinctions keeps people in the present; mindlessness, rules and routines applied regardless of circumstance, can directly cause error (the anti-lock brake example) [BT] (Ch 5, p. 5-12).
- **High reliability organisations**: Perrow's *Normal Accidents*, the Berkeley group's findings (organisations that reinvent themselves, decisions that migrate to the lowest level, commitment to learning, no punishment for honest mistakes), and Weick and Sutcliffe's five characteristics of collective mindfulness (preoccupation with failure, reluctance to simplify, sensitivity to operations, commitment to resilience, deference to expertise), including the point that HROs give strong responses to weak signals [BT] (Ch 5, pp. 5-12 to 5-16).
- **Resilience engineering** (Hollnagel, Woods): failures against a background of success had latent contributors arising from finite resources, uncertainty and constant change, and researchers identified a drift toward failure that precedes major events as planned controls erode under production pressure and change [BT] (Ch 5, p. 5-16, endnotes 24–25); HROs do not treat past success as grounds for confidence [BT] (Ch 5, p. 5-17).
- **Organisational resilience**: the ability to handle disruptions outside the design envelope; resilience needs anticipation, attention and response, continuously exercised, plus time to respond, and a constant sense of unease against complacency [BT] (Ch 5, pp. 5-17 to 5-18, endnotes 26–29).
- **Performance improvement in the workplace**: CRM in aviation, simulators in medicine, aviation and nuclear power, the U.S. Navy and Coast Guard, and INPO's Human Performance Fundamentals training in the mid-1990s [BT] (Ch 5, pp. 5-18 to 5-19).

The chapter closes with the human performance strategy in three parts: reduce the frequency of events by anticipating, preventing and catching active errors; minimise their severity by eliminating latent weaknesses that weaken controls; and cultivate "an environment where honest errors can be openly reported and learned from" [V] (Ch 5, p. 5-19). Experience showing that most causes of human performance problems lie in the work environment "does not relieve individuals of their responsibility to work safety and reliably" [V] (Ch 5, p. 5-19; "safety" is the source's word).

## Part VI: Glossary (selected definitions)

The glossary gives the handbook's working definitions [AP] (Glossary, pp. i–ix).
