Among them: **critical step**, "A procedure step, series of steps, or action that, if performed improperly, will cause irreversible harm to equipment, people, or the environment" [V] (Glossary, p. ii); **lapse**, "An error due to a failure of memory or recall" [V] (Glossary, p. v); **slip**, "A physical action different than intended" [V] (Glossary, p. viii); **latent organizational condition or weakness**, "Undetected deficiencies in organizational processes, equipment, or values that create job-site conditions that either provoke error or degrade the integrity of controls" [V] (Glossary, p. v); **near miss**, a situation that could have had undesirable consequences but did not, ranging from minor breaches to incidents where all safeguards were defeated without loss [AP] (Glossary, p. vi); **positive control**, "Active measure(s) to ensure that what is intended to happen is what happens, and that is all that happens" [V] (Glossary, p. vii); **shortcut**, an action perceived as more efficient that accomplishes the intent rather than the directed actions [AP] (Glossary, p. viii); **uneasiness**, "An attitude of apprehension and wariness regarding the capacity to err when performing specific human actions on plant components" [V] (Glossary, p. ix); and **human error**, "A phrase that generally means the slips, lapses, and mistakes of humankind" [V] (Glossary, p. iv).

## Positions the author explicitly frames against

- *Human performance as a worker-only problem.* The "traditional belief" that failures enter only through unreliable people, so removing "a few bad performers" fixes things; experience shows organisational weaknesses are involved in most events (Ch 1, p. 1-11).
- *Retraining as the default fix for slips and lapses.* Calls retraining for skill-based errors "a waste of time" and "an insult to the worker" (Ch 2, p. 2-27).
- *"Pay attention" as a remedy.* "Avoiding error is not as simple as telling someone to “pay attention.”" (Ch 2, p. 2-19).
- *Equating knowledge-based mode with knowledgeable people's work.* Warns against calling research or one-of-a-kind work knowledge-based because the people are highly educated (Ch 2, p. 2-25).
- *Error reduction alone.* Focusing only on error reduction to prevent events is "a bad strategy", because it only lengthens the time between events (Ch 3, p. 3-3).
- *"Inattention to detail" and "not following procedures" as root causes.* Rejected as root causes despite their common use in the DOE complex (Ch 3, p. 3-22).
- *Investigation that asks who caused the event.* Root cause analysis should ask what could have prevented it; analysis fixated on individual culpability will not find effective corrective actions (Ch 3, p. 3-22).
- *The assumption that careless action reflects poor motivation.* Calls it "a faulty assumption" (Ch 3, p. 3-15) and describes the blame cycle it drives (Ch 4, p. 4-23).
- *Judging people by consequence rather than intent.* Criticises organisations that name, blame, shame and retrain on consequence, and that let violations slide until an event (Ch 4, pp. 4-23 to 4-24).
- *Disciplining honest mistakes.* Listed as a flawed cultural control (Ch 3, p. 3-10).
- *HPI as a programme.* Distinguishes HPI from programmes such as Six Sigma and TQM (Preface, p. v; Ch 1, p. 1-1).
- *Treating work as routine.* "There are no routine tasks" (Ch 2, p. 2-33).

## Citation and source-integrity notes

**Conversion.** PDF (175 pages, 3.5 MB, SHA-256 `82546e3f…66f400e8`) converted with `markitdown 0.1.5` (deterministic; no model-mediated extraction). Post-conversion check: 66,354 words against 64,289 words from `pdftotext` on the same PDF, about 380 words per page; the first page (cover), the last page (concluding material, with the area-office list) and every chapter, attachment, appendix and endnote list are present; no truncation marker. The handbook's page footers (for example `2-27`) survive as standalone lines and are the citation anchors; running headers ("Department of Energy / Human Performance Handbook / Chapter N …") repeat on every page.

**Conversion damage, and how it was handled.** Body prose converted cleanly. Two-column layouts did not: the ISM–HPI integration table (Ch 1, pp. 1-6 to 1-9) and the production/prevention sidebar (Ch 4, p. 4-12) interleave columns, and figures (Anatomy of an Event, information-processing model, GEMS flowchart, SRK chart, Reliability of Controls, Performance Model, Performance Improvement Model, blame cycle, consequence model, BEM leverage chart, resilient-organisation model) survive only as repeated or scattered text fragments; the Culpability Decision Tree's box text survives in order but without its arrows. No `[V]` quotation in this reference is taken from an interleaved table, sidebar or figure; those passages are paraphrased from the parts whose reading order is clear. Some bullet lists lose their bullets or separate from their lead-in.

**Third-party material.** See the header line. All `[V]` quotations are the handbook's own prose. Material reprinted or adapted with permission (Gilbert's BEM via ISPI; Mager and Pipe's gap analysis), material the handbook says it derives from INPO, and passages it quotes or adapts from named authors are paraphrased and marked `[BT]`.

**Source inconsistencies, recorded as found.** The Preface names Chapter 5 "Organizations at Work", but the chapter is titled "Human Performance Evolution" (Preface, p. v; Ch 5, p. 5-1). Chapter 3's running footer reads "Managing Defenses" while its heading reads "Managing Controls". Cross-references point to the wrong chapter in places: Chapter 2 places organisational culture in "Chapter 5" (p. 2-29) and Chapter 3 calls "Culture and Leadership" Chapter 5 (p. 3-10), when both are in Chapter 4; Chapter 5 says Chapter 4 discusses tools for locating latent weaknesses (p. 5-12), which Chapter 3 does. Chapter 2 refers to "Chapter of this handbook" with the number missing (p. 2-34). Chapter 4 refers to its attachments as "Appendix A/B/C" (pp. 4-16, 4-25, 4-26) though they are titled Attachments, and places the BEM tables on "pages 4-15 through 4-18" when they fall on pp. 4-19 to 4-22. The blank page after p. 2-49 is numbered "2-1". The working-memory span is given as "7+1 or -2" on p. 2-2 and "7 + 2" on p. 2-18. The two statements of the strategic formula differ ("Re + Mc → ØE", p. 1-16; "Re + Mc = ØE", p. 2-34). Endnote 43 (Ch 2) indicates an unnamed writer who was the Hanford 200-area training manager at the time of the pump incident; the handbook names no individual author.

**Citation style.** `(Ch N, p. N-M)` using the handbook's printed page numbers, chosen because the converted text preserves them as footers on every page.
